examples.text: A double rainbow isn't magic or a lucky omen, it's just science! It's beautiful light bouncing inside raindrops.
A sandstorm carries heavy sand grains close to the ground, while a dust storm lifts fine dust much higher into the air!
Science starts with good questions like 'Why?' and 'How?' — they push us to investigate and search for answers.
With your teacher, ask: can folded paper stand up? Try folding a sheet, test it on the table, and change the fold. Describe what happened. Asking and trying materials are parts of science.

How do we measure the length of things?

We use a ruler to measure length in centimeters or meters!
A ruler is a handy tool for measuring length! It has centimeter and millimeter marks to show exactly how long an object is.

Why do scientists use a hand lens or ruler when they already have eyes?

Because tools like hand lenses and rulers extend the senses! They help us see tiny details and measure length more accurately than our eyes alone.
Scissors are used to cut cloth, paper, cardboard, and other thin materials.
With your teacher, compare an empty balloon with an inflated one. A balloon stretches as air goes inside. It helps you observe that air takes up space.
Modeling clay can be pressed and shaped into simple models during a science activity. You can reshape the same clay to compare a ball with a flat shape.

How can small pieces of cardboard become one big useful thing?

When you join pieces with tape or glue, they stick together and form a larger, stronger object. Joining changes the size and shape of the material!

How do scientists observe carefully?

They look, listen, and touch carefully! Then, they write down exactly what they notice without adding any guesses.

How do scientists predict and check?

They use what they know to guess what happens next in a test, then they measure to check!
A ruler is a straight tool with centimeter and millimeter marks — perfect for measuring how long something is!
A ruler is a handy tool for measuring length! It has centimeter and millimeter marks to show exactly how long an object is.

How do we measure the length of things?

We use a ruler to measure length in centimeters or meters!
A tape measure is a flexible tool marked in units like centimeters and meters to measure the length of things!
For measuring how long things are, the meter (m) is the SI base unit of length.
The meter is the perfect unit for measuring length or distance! We use it every day.
The Mohs scale measures how hard it is to scratch a mineral!
The hardness of a mineral simply means how hard it is to scratch!
Silk thread gets woven into cloth that is smooth and shiny.
The milkfish has a long, sleek body covered in shiny, silver-colored scales.
Stretch a rubber band too far and it won't return to shape — it may snap!
A spider's dragline silk stretches a little under its weight, softening a fall without breaking.
Recycling reduces pollution! When we recycle, less trash is burned or left in nature to harm our air and water.
Burning dried leaves releases fine particulate matter into the air! Avoid breathing it in to prevent coughing and asthma attacks.
The Philippines sends a lot of plastic into the ocean because waste isn't managed well.
Recycling reduces pollution! When we recycle, less trash is burned or left in nature to harm our air and water.

How can we help reduce pollution?

Buy less plastic and reuse what we already have!
In the Philippines, many junk shops buy old bottles, cans, and newspapers to send to factories that will reuse them!

Why can't we pour used cooking oil down the sink?

Oil can clog the pipes and harm the environment, so it should be sealed in a container and thrown in the garbage.
Recycling means making new things out of old waste, like making new paper from used paper!
Always separate your paper from other trash! Putting it in its own bin makes it super easy to recycle.
When glass breaks, it forms sharp edges that can cut you! Always handle broken glass very carefully.
Factories add broken glass, called cullet, to the mix! It melts easier, saving heat and fuel. That makes recycling bottles doubly helpful for our planet!
Metals are malleable — you can bend or hammer them into new shapes without breaking!
Many plastics get soft and squishy when heated, making it super easy to mold them into different shapes!
The paper in your notebook is made from tiny wood fibers mashed into pulp, pressed flat, and dried!
Coconut oil is made by pressing copra — the dried meat of the coconut — to squeeze out the fat stored inside as oil!
Metals are malleable — you can bend or hammer them into new shapes without breaking!
An anvil is a heavy, solid metal tool! It provides a hard surface for hammering and shaping other heated metals.

How can small pieces of cardboard become one big useful thing?

When you join pieces with tape or glue, they stick together and form a larger, stronger object. Joining changes the size and shape of the material!
The hard trunk of an old coconut tree is cut into "coco lumber," used as posts and boards for building houses.
Even if you change an object's shape, it stays the same material! If you fold or cut paper, it is still paper.
Iron ore is melted to get iron, which is then made into steel for buildings and vehicles!
Iron is a super strong metal! We use it to build tall buildings, big bridges, and vehicles.
Did you know gold never rusts? Even after many years, it keeps its beautiful shine!
Gold (Au) is a beautiful transition metal that we commonly use to make lovely jewelry!
Long ago, people used silver as money and coins because it was super valuable and easy to carry around!
Silver slowly turns dark when exposed to air. That's why it needs polishing to bring back its beautiful shine!
The wires in your house are made of copper because it conducts electricity super well!
Copper is a superstar at conducting electricity, which is why it is commonly used in electrical wires!
Observing is a science process skill that uses your senses to describe things around you.
Predicting is a science process skill where you use careful observations and patterns to make a smart guess about what will happen next.

With your teacher, observe a small plant and measure its height in centimeters. Predict whether it will grow taller. Care for it normally, then measure again after several days. Record both heights and compare your prediction with what you observed.
Measuring is a science process skill that uses units like millimeters, centimeters, and meters to describe the size of objects.

A carabao pulls a wooden cart — are they both alive?

Nope! The carabao eating grass is living, but the wooden cart is non-living — it can't eat or grow!

Is coral a rock or a plant?

Neither! Coral is actually made of tiny living animals called polyps.

Is coral a rock or something alive?

Surprise — coral is actually a living animal, not a rock, even though it feels hard like one!
A giraffe can grow about 5 to 6 meters tall!
An ostrich can grow to stand about 2.5 meters tall.

Why do we feel pain when we get hurt?

Nerves in your skin send pain signals to warn you of danger, so you can react and stay safe.

Do roots grow toward water too?

Yes — besides growing downward, roots also grow toward moist soil, a response called hydrotropism.
Rats multiply fast because they have many babies, often!
Some animals, like chickens and other birds, make babies by laying eggs.
A frog's strong, long back legs are what let it jump so far!
A human has exactly two legs — perfect for standing tall and walking around!
Many insects have wings that let them fly through the air.
Swifts have long, narrow wings shaped perfectly for flying very fast.
A bird's beak shape matches the kind of food it eats!
A Komodo dragon uses its forked tongue to smell prey from far away.
Rats use their long tail to keep their balance while climbing.
Milkfish are strong, fast swimmers thanks to their wide, forked tail.
Roots soak up water and nutrients from the soil so the plant can stay alive and grow.
A plant's roots soak up water and nutrients from the soil so the whole plant can use them.
The stem carries water up from the roots all the way to the leaves.
A tree trunk is really just a big, hard, woody stem — it still carries water all the way up even in a very tall tree.

Which plant part makes food?

The leaf! It makes food for the plant through photosynthesis, using sunlight.

What job does a plant's stem do?

It carries water from the roots up to the leaves, and sends food back down to the rest of the plant!
A seed needs three things to sprout: water, warmth, and air.
All animals, including us humans, need oxygen to stay alive.
Dogs need clean food, fresh water, and good care to stay healthy.
A pregnant mother needs healthy, nutritious food so her baby can grow strong inside her womb.
A seed needs three things to sprout: water, warmth, and air.
Most rice grows in fields flooded with water, called paddies.
Cloud rats shelter and rest in holes or hollows inside old, large trees.
Forest trees like the narra become homes for birds and many other animals.
Earthworms are food for birds, chickens, and other animals.
Fallen leaves rot away and turn into food that makes the soil rich.
Fallen leaves rot away and turn into food that makes the soil rich.
To grow tall and healthy, corn needs sunlight, water, and good soil.
Planting narra trees helps bring back forests that have been cut down.
When trees come back, birds, animals, and insects finally get their homes back too!
Planting narra trees helps bring back forests that have been cut down.
Along many coasts in the Philippines, people replant mangroves to protect the shoreline.
A wind turbine spins when the wind blows, and that spinning motion generates electricity!

What happens when wind pushes against a turbine's blades?

The blades spin and turn the machine!
A river current spins a water wheel on its axle, transferring power to grind grain in a mill!
Flowing water has a strong force that can push things, just like how it can turn a water wheel!
You use a push when you close a door or push a cart!
When you push or pull a door open, you are using force in both actions!
When you push or pull a door open, you are using force in both actions!
Farmers use the carabao to pull a plow and break up the soil in rice fields.
A kalesa is a carriage pulled by a horse—the horse uses muscle power to apply force and make the wheels roll!

Why is a wheel always round?

A wheel is round so it can roll easily! If it were square, it would bump and get stuck — no rolling at all!
People can move objects by pushing, pulling, carrying, lifting, or blowing on them.

With your teacher, compare how toy balls roll or bounce. Record each ball’s size and material, such as rubber or wood. A bigger ball has a different size; a wooden ball has a different material from a rubber one. Consider both features before explaining the movement.

Why is a wheel always round?

A wheel is round so it can roll easily! If it were square, it would bump and get stuck — no rolling at all!
To catch the most water, keep the wide blade flat against the water as you pull! If it's sideways, it just slices through and pushes very little.
A tortoise moves slowly because its shell is heavy and its legs are short.
Even though a ferry full of passengers is heavy, it floats! The water pushes it upward against its large, hollow hull.

With your teacher, compare how toy balls roll or bounce. Record each ball’s size and material, such as rubber or wood. A bigger ball has a different size; a wooden ball has a different material from a rubber one. Consider both features before explaining the movement.
Playing sungka on a smooth wooden board reduces friction, allowing the little shells to slide easily right into the holes!

Why is it harder to slide on rough ground?

Rough surfaces make more friction than smooth surfaces!
A ball rolling on grass stops faster than on smooth tile! The rough grass creates more friction to slow it down.
Objects can move closer to or farther from their original position in relation to a reference point.
Objects can move to the left or to the right in relation to their original position.
To measure distance, mark the starting position and final position of a moving object, then use a ruler or tape measure to find the length between them.
A drum makes sound because its stretched skin vibrates when you strike it!
Longer or thicker strings vibrate more slowly, so they make a lower pitch!
Sound travels down your narrow ear canal until it reaches your eardrum.
An elephant blows air through its trunk to make a big, loud trumpet sound!
Some things like the sun, fire, candles, and light bulbs make their own light all by themselves!
A gasera is a lamp that draws kerosene up a wick. It gives light when the kerosene burns at the flame!

Why does sunlight make a room feel warm?

Sunlight coming through a window carries heat that warms up the inside of the room!
A mirror doesn't make its own light — it only bounces back light that's already there. So in a dark room with no light, you'll see nothing in the mirror!
Indoors, you can make a shadow using a flashlight and an object that blocks its light!
A wooden block casts a dark shadow because its opaque surface completely blocks straight-traveling light rays from a flashlight!
Without light there is no shadow; light is needed for a shadow to exist!
A shadow gets bigger when the object is moved closer to the light source!
Very loud sounds can damage the tiny parts inside your ear and weaken your hearing.
Too much sun can burn your skin — that's why wearing a hat or sunblock outside is so important!
Ultraviolet light from the sun causes sunburn, which makes our skin turn red and get damaged!
Never shine a laser pointer into eyes! Even a small, cheap laser can injure the eye's retina.
Raising or lowering a colored flag is a movement-and-color signal! People use it so a far partner can easily see a yes or a no.

Do movement, sound, and light always send information?

Only if both people agreed on the code first! A random blink or sound does not yet mean a specific word.

How does a toy string telephone work?

Sound travels through the solid string that connects the two cans!
In a tin-can telephone, sound travels along the tight string as vibrations — like a secret message highway!
In 1880, Alexander Graham Bell invented the photophone! This amazing device transmitted sound using a bright beam of sunlight.
Optical fiber cables carry internet data as rapid pulses of light inside thin glass strands! This is faster and loses less signal than copper wire.

With your teacher, observe non-living things around school. Look for soil, rocks, water, and clouds from a safe place. Draw or describe what you find and where it is. Observe unfamiliar materials without touching or tasting them.
Dark, thick clouds are full of water! They are a clear sign that rain is coming soon.
Clouds come in fun shapes! Cumulus look like fluffy cotton balls, stratus form flat layers, and cirrus are high and wispy.
Iron ore is melted to get iron, which is then made into steel for buildings and vehicles!
Did you know cardboard is just a thick kind of paper? It is also made from tiny wood fibers!
Air is an earth material you can't hold like a pebble, but it fills the space around every living thing!
Clay is a sticky earth material made of tiny mineral bits. It's non-living, even when people shape it into pots!
A weather chart tracks if it's sunny, rainy, or cloudy every day, helping us spot patterns in the weather!
When we record weather instrument readings every day, we can spot cool patterns, like exactly when the rainy or dry season arrives!
A weather chart tracks if it's sunny, rainy, or cloudy every day, helping us spot patterns in the weather!
At midday, the sun is highest with direct rays. But the hottest time is mid-afternoon—the ground and air need time to warm up!
Never wade or play in floodwater — staying out of it is the best way to avoid leptospirosis!
Drink plenty of water during El Niño dry spells to prevent heatstroke when temperatures exceed 35°C!
Heavy monsoon rains often cause rapid flash floods in low-lying areas of Metro Manila!
Never wade or play in floodwater — staying out of it is the best way to avoid leptospirosis!

Can we only see the Moon at night?

Nope! Sometimes, we can also see the Moon in the bright daytime sky!
The moon is sometimes visible in daytime because it's bright and in the right spot! It's up during the day as often as at night, just harder to see.
The dark patches we see on the Moon are wide, flat plains of old, hardened lava!
The Moon doesn't make its own light! It just shines by reflecting the bright light from the Sun.
You can spot five planets with just your eyes — no telescope needed! They are Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
That bright "star" you see after sunset or before sunrise isn't a star at all! It's actually Venus, the brightest planet in our sky.
Sirius is the brightest star we can see in the night sky!
When you look up at the night sky, the brightest star you will see is Sirius!
Want to track the Moon? Draw its spot next to a bright star! You'll see it shift eastward every single night.

Where does the sun set every day?

The sun always sets in the West!
Just like the Sun, the Moon rises in the east and sets in the west because of Earth's rotation!
Morning sunlight helps our bodies make vitamin D! This special vitamin gives us super strong and healthy bones.
Stay away from the shoreline during a spring tide, as the aligned Sun and Moon create unusually high, dangerous waves!
Long before GPS, sailors used fixed stars in the night sky as their trusty guide to find direction at sea!
Lost at night? Look up for the North Star, Polaris! It points to true north to help you navigate back safely.
Too much sun can burn your skin — that's why wearing a hat or sunblock outside is so important!
Drink plenty of water and stay in the shade when the heat index exceeds 40°C to prevent heatstroke!
Never look straight at the Sun during a solar eclipse, because those bright rays can damage your eyes!

Why shouldn't we stare at the sun?

We should never stare straight at the sun because it can damage our eyes!
